b: Rewarded video is an advertising format in which a person chooses to watch a short, usually full-screen video and receives a reward for finishing it: coins in a game, an extra life, a hint, an hour of ad-free listening or access to an article. The format exists because most mobile games and many apps give their product away and earn money from a small minority of paying users. Rewarded video lets the non-paying majority pay with attention instead of cash, and it does so with consent built in, since nothing plays until the person asks for it.

Google's AdMob help centre states that rewarded ads are served only after a user explicitly chooses to view one. The Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB), in a playbook published on December 5, 2018, called the wider category "opt-in value exchange advertising" and noted that "it is the publisher, not the brand, that owns the reward transaction." The advertiser pays for the impression; the app or site decides what the viewer gets.

The sequence starts inside the product, not in the ad stack. A game designer places an offer at a natural pause: a button reading "Watch an ad for 50 coins" after a failed level, or a prompt to double the winnings from a round.

When the person taps the offer, the app's software development kit (SDK) requests an ad. In most apps that request passes through a mediation layer, which collects bids from several ad networks or ranks them in a mediation waterfall and returns the highest-paying ad.

The video then plays full screen. According to Google's AdMob documentation, a countdown runs for between 5 and 30 seconds depending on the creative, and the reward is granted when it ends. By default AdMob may serve an ad pod of two videos back to back for one impression; publishers can exclude pods, though Google warns this "may impact ad revenue". Creatives need not be video at all: AdMob's rewarded units also accept static images and interactive units such as playable ads and surveys, with interactive formats switched on by default.

Closing early forfeits the reward, and most platforms show a warning before the person leaves. When the countdown completes, the SDK fires a callback and the app credits the reward. Because a client-side callback can be spoofed, larger publishers also use server-side verification (SSV): the ad server sends a signed request to a URL the publisher controls, and the reward is credited only when that call arrives.
Rewards are configured in the ad platform as a unit name and amount, so a studio can change them without shipping a new app version.
Rewarded video on the open web

Rewarded formats are not limited to apps. Google Ad Manager supports rewarded ads for web, and its help centre sets out the mechanics. The publisher builds the opt-in screen and delivers the reward. The Google Publisher Tag (GPT) exposes three events, rewardedSlotReady, rewardedSlotGranted and rewardedSlotClosed, and the page must call makeRewardedVisible() to start the ad. Only one rewarded slot may request at a time. The default reward is "1 reward", editable by type and amount. An impression counts once the ad appears. A display creative must remain visible for 7 seconds before the reward is granted.

Rewarded web inventory can be sold through reservations, Preferred Deals, Private Auctions, Programmatic Guaranteed and the open auction. In bid requests, OpenRTB, the auction protocol maintained by IAB Tech Lab, flags the placement with an impression attribute called rwdd, set to 1 when the user receives a reward. The attribute arrived in OpenRTB 2.6, published in April 2022.

The best-known web use is Google's Offerwall, which asks a visitor who has read a set number of pages to watch a rewarded ad or take another action to continue. Ad Manager launched it on June 26, 2025 and AdSense made it generally available on April 13, 2026, with the rewarded ad as the default choice.

Durations cluster between 15 and 30 seconds, but platforms allow longer. In February 2025 AdMob introduced an app-level high-engagement setting covering interstitial and rewarded units. With it disabled, rewarded ads are capped at 30 seconds and need one step to exit; with it enabled, the cap rises to 60 seconds and exiting can take three steps. Roblox, which opened its own rewarded format in 2025, described ads of "up to 30-second" length. Discord's Video Quests grant a reward after about 15 seconds.
Frequency caps are set by the publisher, often per user per day, because each reward adds currency to a game economy.

Rewarded advertising in mobile grew out of offerwalls, which from around 2010 paid players virtual currency for installing apps or completing offers. Tapjoy, Supersonic and Fyber are named as early operators in a January 2026 history by Mistplay, itself a rewarded-app company. Game-focused video networks, including AdColony, which launched in March 2011, Vungle, Chartboost, AppLovin and Unity Ads, then made short video the main reward trigger.

Apple shaped the format early. In June 2014 it briefly rejected apps offering rewarded video before narrowing its rule, according to TechCrunch: rewards for watching ads were acceptable, rewards for downloading other apps were not.

Google brought the format into AdMob on March 17, 2016, at the Game Developers Conference. Arun Balaraman, group product manager for AdMob, announced rewarded video mediation with AdColony, AppLovin, Chartboost, Fyber, Upsight and Vungle; a developer post on March 31 added Unity Ads. In March 2017 Google's "Rewarded 101" guide described the format as "non-intrusive, short-form video". In July 2017 AppLift and Adjust ran a webinar on rewarded ads, defined as publishers rewarding users "with in-app items for watching video ads".

The format widened from 2018. Google Play opened rewarded products in beta on March 6, 2019, according to VentureBeat, letting developers launch rewarded video from the Play Console without an extra SDK. AdMob later added rewarded interstitials, still labelled beta in its help centre as of November 2026. OpenRTB 2.6 standardised the rwdd flag in 2022.

Gaming platforms then built their own supply. Roblox launched rewarded video at the IAB Playfronts on April 1, 2025, with Google as programmatic partner, and said early tests averaged completion above 80%. By its July 31, 2025 earnings call, the product was leaving beta with nearly 100 publishers. In January 2026 Magnite secured exclusive global rights to Roblox rewarded video on mobile in-app, after PubMatic in 2024 and Google in 2025.

For brands, rewarded video promises something rare in digital media: a viewer who asked for the ad. Completion is the headline metric. Roblox reported completion "exceeding 90%" and 95% viewability across more than 1,000 brands in its fourth-quarter 2025 shareholder letter. Discord cites a 97% median completion rate for Quests, based on internal data to June 30, 2026.

For app publishers, rewarded video tends to earn the highest prices of any in-app format. Appodeal's report covering October to December 2024, drawn from more than 100,000 apps and 70 ad networks, found rewarded video had "the highest eCPM across both platforms" - effective cost per mille (eCPM) being revenue per thousand impressions -, with banners lowest and iOS ahead of Android in every format.

The strongest criticism concerns incentivised attention. A viewer who watches to earn coins may leave the phone on the table while the countdown runs. High completion is partly a design artefact: the reward is released at the end, so completion is close to guaranteed in rewarded video and says little about whether anyone paid attention.

Measurement blind spots are a second problem. From August 20 to August 28, 2026, rewarded video failed to play in AdMob-served Android apps, showing a static play icon. Google logged it at the lowest severity tier and published no impression or revenue figures. PPC Land's analysis noted that an auction can win while rendering fails, so fill and eCPM dashboards can look healthy during an outage.

There are user experience and child-safety concerns too. Longer durations and multi-step exits, permitted under AdMob's high-engagement setting, sit uneasily with the format's voluntary premise. Rewards in children's games raise policy questions, and AdMob applies automatic adjustments to apps in Google's Families programme. Roblox reported that 35% of age-verified users at January 31, 2026 were under 13.
Finally, platform rules remain fluid. PPC Land's coverage of Google's Offerwall recorded publisher complaints that machine-learning optimisation was switched on without asking first.
Rewarded interstitial. Plays at a natural transition without an explicit opt-in. AdMob requires an intro screen announcing the reward and a clear way to skip, and serves only skippable ads.
Interstitial video. A full-screen ad shown between screens with no reward and no choice.
Offerwall. A menu of tasks, such as installs, surveys or levels reached, each paying currency. Rewarded video may appear as one option.
Rewarded user acquisition. A buy-side channel in which advertisers pay reward apps for installs or in-app events. Rewarded video is a monetisation format, not an acquisition channel.

Discord opened auction-priced Video Quests on September 29, 2026, replacing fixed prices with dynamic pricing and planning fully self-serve buying for early 2027; the reservation version was renamed Video Quests Reserve. Google Ad Manager added server-side verification for rewarded web inventory from October 29, 2026, letting publishers validate reward events on websites as they already could in apps.

Who: App and game publishers, website owners using Google Ad Manager or AdSense, ad networks and mediation platforms such as AdMob, AppLovin, Unity and Liftoff, supply-side platforms such as Magnite and PubMatic, and gaming platforms including Roblox and Discord.
What: An opt-in ad format in which a person watches a short video, or an image or playable unit, and receives a reward set by the publisher, such as currency, lives or content access.

When: It grew from mobile offerwalls around 2010, entered AdMob mediation in March 2016, was standardised in OpenRTB 2.6 in April 2022, and expanded to Roblox in 2025 and Discord's auction in September 2026.
Where: Mostly in mobile games and apps, increasingly on websites through Google's rewarded web ads and Offerwall, and on gaming platforms.

Why: It lets non-paying users fund free products with attention, gives publishers their highest-priced in-app impressions, and gives advertisers near-complete views, though completion driven by a reward says little about attention.
